nodes.label: A0 · Elder tradition
nodes.definition: Organised reciprocity on this continent is older than the Republic. Indigenous nations ran complete economies of mutual obligation, and the United States tried to outlaw them by name.

argument.warrant: If a complete system of reciprocal care was operating before the Republic, was outlawed by the Republic's own government, and is still operating today, then the American mutual aid story does not begin in 1787. It begins on a continent where organised reciprocity was already complete.
argument.qualifier: This chapter is about sovereign nations' own traditions. They are the elder context of American mutual aid, not an early draft of it.
argument.rebuttal: One could object that Indigenous reciprocity belongs to separate sovereign histories, not to the American civic story.
argument.answer: But the United States wrote itself into this history when it made the feasts punishable offences at every agency in 1883 and entered the reasoning into the record. A tradition the Republic legislated against, and that outlasted the statute, is part of the Republic's story on the government's own evidence.
grounds: On the Northwest Coast, the potlatch worked as a complete economic institution. A household's giving created standing claims it could call on when its fishing failed or its house burned, so the feast system served as insurance, redistribution, and public record at once.

The United States outlawed this economy in documents that survive. The Rules Governing the Court of Indian Offenses of 1883 made the feasts punishable by withheld rations and imprisonment, the federal dance bans were not lifted until 1934, and the right to practise was affirmed in law only in 1978.

The tradition still operates. In 2020 the Navajo & Hopi Families COVID-19 Relief Fund, organised by Navajo and Hopi women, delivered food and water across the Navajo Nation and raised eighteen million dollars in its first year. Its leads told the Navajo Times that the fund ran on the old kinship ethic of k'é.

nodes.label: A1 · Parallel founding of 1787
nodes.definition: Organised mutual aid in the United States is as old as the constitutional Republic. The Free African Society, 1787, Philadelphia, is the earliest documented formally organised network.

argument.warrant: If organised mutual aid was founded in the same city and season as the Constitution, then it is not a later patch on the American system. The two institutions are the same age, and the history should date them together.
argument.qualifier: The Free African Society was not the first organisation of its kind. The claim rests on documentation: its charter survives and can be dated precisely, while older traditions, Indigenous and enslaved, rarely entered the written record.
argument.rebuttal: One could object that a society of a few dozen members in one city is too small to count as a founding.
argument.answer: But the meeting a few blocks away was fifty-five delegates, and both meetings matter for what grew from them. By 1838 more than a hundred societies had been built on the Philadelphia pattern, and by 1920 the tradition reached one in three adult American men.
grounds: The Free African Society was founded on 12 April 1787 in Philadelphia, weeks before the Constitutional Convention met in the same city. Its founding charter, the Preamble and Articles of Association, survives in print.

The charter's terms were reciprocal, not charitable. Each member paid one shilling a month into a common fund that supported the sick, buried the dead, and provided for widows and fatherless children, under rules the members wrote and governed themselves.

When yellow fever killed roughly one in ten Philadelphians in 1793, the society's members stayed, nursed the sick, and buried the dead for Black and white residents alike. Its founders defended that record in a pamphlet that became the first federal copyright obtained by African Americans.

The design spread. W.E.B. Du Bois's 1907 study, Economic Co-operation Among Negro Americans, records that surveys of 1838 already counted roughly a hundred such societies, and it traces the same dues-and-benefits pattern across the country over the following decades.

nodes.label: A2 · Parallel civic infrastructure
nodes.definition: Excluded communities built mutual aid as the primary social safety net — healthcare, insurance, burial, education — that the state and market denied them.

grounds: The Free African Society's design — dues, sickness benefits, burial provision — repeated in Charleston's Brown Fellowship Society (1790) and the New York African Society for Mutual Relief (1808).
Chinese huiguan consolidated as the Six Companies, Jewish landsmanshaftn, Italian società di mutuo soccorso, and Mexican sociedades mutualistas each independently built the same institution.
Du Bois's 1907 survey documented these organisations in the thousands as the principal provider of insurance, healthcare, education, and burial for Black Americans.
Public relief before the New Deal was local, discretionary, and racially exclusionary, so the societies were the system, not a supplement to it.
argument.warrant: If the same institutional design appears independently wherever exclusion created the same need, the pattern is structural: excluded communities built the safety net because no one else would.
argument.qualifier: Coverage varied by city and era; the societies did not reach everyone, and some enforced their own exclusions.
argument.rebuttal: These were private ethnic clubs, not civic infrastructure.
argument.answer: They performed the functions we now call the safety net — insurance, healthcare, burial, education — at documented scale, for communities the public system excluded by design.

nodes.label: A3 · Fraternal scale
nodes.definition: By 1920 roughly one in three adult American men belonged to a fraternal order that paid sickness, death, and burial benefits — the largest voluntary association system after the churches.

grounds: By 1920, on the most conservative estimate, one in three adult American men belonged to a fraternal order, and through auxiliaries and juvenile branches the orders reached wives and children as well.

Provision was the orders' central business. Around 1910 a lodge contract bought a family a year of medical care for roughly two dollars, about a day's wage, and the societies also built sanitariums, orphanages, and homes for the elderly while fraternal life insurance grew into a major share of all coverage in force.

The design served both sides of the colour line. When the white Odd Fellows refused Black applicants, Peter Ogden obtained a charter from the order's English parent in 1843, and the Grand United Order of Odd Fellows grew into one of the largest Black organisations in the country.

The scale drew organised opposition. The Journal of the American Medical Association ran attacks on 'the lodge practice evil' in the early 1900s, and county medical societies punished physicians who accepted lodge contracts, because collective bargaining drove fees down.
argument.warrant: An arrangement that enrolled a third of the country's men and did the work of insurance, medicine, and burial was not a fringe experiment. Before any federal safety net existed, this was how ordinary Americans organised their security.
argument.qualifier: The one-in-three figure is the most conservative estimate and counts adult men only. The orders were segregated, and the claim is about scale and function, not inclusiveness.
argument.rebuttal: One could object that the fraternal orders were social clubs in costumes, and that the benefits were a sideline to the ritual.
argument.answer: But the regalia decorated a working insurance system. Provision was the orders' central business, and organised medicine attacked lodge practice precisely because it worked well enough to drive doctors' fees down.

nodes.label: B1 · New Deal displacement
nodes.definition: New Deal social insurance replaced community provision and was narrated as filling a vacuum, not as taking over what lodges already did.

grounds: When the Social Security Act was signed in 1935, fraternal societies were still the leading providers of social welfare in the United States, and their membership had reached an estimated half of the adult male population at its height.

Depression-era communities organised new provision on a large scale before federal relief reached them. The Bureau of Labor Statistics surveyed the nation's cooperative self-help enterprises in 1933, and Black communities, largely excluded from relief administration, ran a parallel cooperative surge through churches and long-standing societies.

After 1935 the societies' core products, sick benefits, old-age funds, and widows' payments, were offered by the state and funded by payroll taxes that members paid whether they kept their lodge or not. Fraternal membership fell and kept falling, and the welfare functions went first.

The standard surveys of American welfare history frame the story as a run from the poor law to the welfare state, with community provision as a curiosity along the way. Andrew Morris notes that Michael Katz's leading synthesis of the field devotes three pages to voluntary agencies after the Second World War.
argument.warrant: If functioning mutual institutions were the country's leading welfare providers on the day the Act was signed, then the story of a state arriving in an empty room is wrong on its own terms. What happened was replacement, and replacement is a different story from rescue.
argument.qualifier: The lodges could not have carried the Depression; the collapse overwhelmed every institution in the country. The claim is about what the New Deal displaced and how the displacement was narrated, not that Social Security was unnecessary.
argument.rebuttal: One could object that the societies were already dying of their own weaknesses: damaged benefit funds, actuarial problems, and changing tastes among the young.
argument.answer: But the timing is not subtle. The welfare functions went first, once the state offered the same products funded by compulsory payroll taxes and commercial insurers took much of what remained, and the social functions built around those benefits followed.

nodes.label: B2 · Civil rights care
nodes.definition: The Civil Rights movement ran on care infrastructure: citizenship schools, church networks, and provision that made sustained protest possible.

grounds: For the 381 days of the Montgomery bus boycott, a parallel transit system of hundreds of cars, dispatchers, and pickup points moved tens of thousands of people to work, funded in part by Georgia Gilmore's Club From Nowhere, a cooks' club organised so that no member could be fired for feeding the movement.

The citizenship schools that Septima Clark and Bernice Robinson opened on Johns Island in 1957 spread across the South, run by local people in kitchens, church basements, and beauty parlours. Hundreds were operating by the mid-1960s, and field organisers repeatedly traced voter registration drives back to them.

When Leflore County, Mississippi cut off federal surplus food for some twenty thousand residents in retaliation for a registration drive, SNCC moved tons of donated food into the Delta and distributed it alongside registration canvassing. Feeding people and registering them became one operation.

The historians who worked closest to the ground, Charles Payne and Barbara Ransby among them, argue that this care infrastructure was the movement's foundation rather than its support system. The field secretaries were housed, fed, and protected by local families, and behind them stood the Black church, a mutual aid institution since the days of the Free African Society.
argument.warrant: Marches last days; the systems that feed, house, teach, and move people run for years. If every set piece of the movement stood on that provision, then the care systems were not background logistics. In long stretches they simply were the movement.
argument.qualifier: This claim reads the movement through its infrastructure. It does not diminish the marches, speeches, and courtrooms; the point is what carried them.
argument.rebuttal: One could object that cooking, driving, and teaching are the ordinary logistics of any campaign, not a civic tradition in their own right.
argument.answer: But the historians closest to the ground concluded the opposite. The slow, relational care work was what Charles Payne calls the organising tradition itself, the model Ella Baker deliberately built SNCC on, and the people who did it kept the movement alive between the famous days.

nodes.label: B3 · Survival programs
nodes.definition: The Black Panther survival programs — breakfast first among them — were mutual aid at civic scale, then watched, disrupted, and later absorbed as state policy.

grounds: In January 1969 the Black Panther Party began serving free breakfast to school children in an Oakland church basement, and the programme spread through the party's chapters until kitchens across the country were feeding thousands of children every school morning.

Breakfast was one programme among many. The party ran free medical clinics in more than a dozen cities, free sickle cell anaemia testing when public health authorities barely acknowledged the disease, free clothing programmes, an ambulance service, and free busing so families could visit the incarcerated.

The FBI's own analysis called the breakfast programme 'the best and most influential activity going for the BPP' and 'potentially the greatest threat' to efforts to neutralise the party. COINTELPRO operations followed: raided breakfast sites, rumours spread to parents that the food was poisoned, and pressure on landlords and suppliers.

While the Bureau worked to destroy the programme, the federal government scaled its model. The School Breakfast Program was expanded through the early 1970s and made permanent in 1975, and the geographer Nik Heynen states plainly that the Panther programme was both the model for and impetus behind the federal programmes now in existence.
argument.warrant: A programme that the FBI's own files called the party's greatest threat, and that the federal government copied into permanent law while dismantling its authors, was neither marginal nor theatre. By the government's own paperwork, it was civic infrastructure that worked.
argument.qualifier: The claim is about the survival programmes and their record, not a verdict on everything the party did or said.
argument.rebuttal: One could object that the programmes were recruitment tools: service delivery in the service of an armed political organisation, not genuine mutual aid.
argument.answer: But recruitment and reciprocity are not exclusive, and the benevolent societies built political life on their common funds too. The record shows children fed every school morning and a model persuasive enough that the state adopted it, and the state's own files say the threat was precisely that it worked.

nodes.label: B4 · AIDS networks
nodes.definition: During the AIDS crisis, care networks kept people alive when official medicine and the state would not.

grounds: In January 1982, six men founded the Gay Men's Health Crisis for an epidemic that did not yet have a name. Within months it had built a volunteer hotline, crisis counselling, legal help, and the buddy programme, which assigned a volunteer to each sick man to cook, clean, and stay present.

The federal government's response was, for years, close to nothing. Research went underfunded, and the President did not deliver a major address on AIDS until 1987, by which time more than twenty thousand Americans had died.

The care came first and the politics rose from it. The community built buddy teams, meal deliveries, food pantries that ran for decades, and open needle exchanges before they were legal, and when ACT UP formed in 1987 it grew out of rooms full of people who had been nursing, burying, and provisioning each other since the epidemic began.

The movement also pooled expertise as mutual aid. Its treatment activists taught themselves virology and biostatistics, audited trial designs, and forced changes in how the FDA approved drugs, an intervention in scientific practice that is now studied in its own right.
argument.warrant: When the federal government answered the century's deadliest epidemic with years of near silence, survival depended on what the community could build. The networks that did that work, and their documented sequence of care first and protest after, are the proof of the claim.
argument.qualifier: The claim concerns the years of official refusal, roughly 1982 to 1987. It does not deny what public medicine and funding later did, once forced.
argument.rebuttal: One could object that volunteer buddy teams and pantries were compassionate stopgaps, marginal next to what real medical institutions eventually delivered.
argument.answer: But the buddy programmes and pantries sustained thousands through the years when no institution would touch them, and the same movement then changed the institutions themselves, forcing reforms in how the FDA approved drugs.

nodes.label: B5 · Maternal networks
nodes.definition: The most pervasive form of mutual aid is maternal and kin care, and it has never been counted as civic infrastructure.

grounds: Martha Ballard's diary, kept from 1785 to 1812, records 816 deliveries and, woven through them, an entire reciprocal care economy that appears in no ledger of the period. Historians dismissed the diary as trivial for a century, until Laurel Thatcher Ulrich's study of it won the Pulitzer Prize.

The scholarship that recovered these networks worked against the grain of the archive. Emily Abel reconstructed nineteenth-century women's reciprocal care from family diaries, and Anne Firor Scott documented women's benevolent associations, including Black women's associations, organising from the 1790s onward.

For women whose care work was also employment, disproportionately Black women in domestic work, mutual aid was organised inside their exclusion from labour law: hiring networks, benefit pools, and training circles that Premilla Nadasen's history recovers, running for decades before any formal union would touch them.

The practice never stopped. Family, friend, and neighbour care remains the backbone of American childcare, larger than the formal daycare sector it subsidises; studies document dense informal networks among low-income single mothers; and when schools closed in 2020, parents assembled learning pods and childcare co-ops within weeks.
argument.warrant: A practice that is reciprocal, organised, and meets needs no institution meets is mutual aid by every definition. If its record is thin, and the thinness traces to record-keepers coding it as women's work rather than civic activity, then the gap measures the archive, not the practice.
argument.qualifier: The claim is about recognition. The scholarship recovering these networks is real, rigorous, and recent, and this page stands on it rather than replacing it.
argument.rebuttal: One could object that family and neighbourly care is private life, not civic infrastructure: every society has mothers helping mothers.
argument.answer: But scale and function say otherwise. Family, friend, and neighbour care carries more American childcare than the formal daycare sector, and when schools closed in 2020 the networks stood up learning pods within weeks. Infrastructure that carries that load is civic whether or not anyone files its minutes.

nodes.label: C1 · Crisis expansion
nodes.definition: In disaster, mutual aid routinely crosses the lines that bound it in ordinary time.

grounds: In 1793, when yellow fever killed a tenth of Philadelphia and the federal government fled its own capital, the Free African Society organised the nursing of the sick and the burial of the dead, and the sick and the dead were overwhelmingly white.

The crossing recurs wherever catastrophe lands. After Katrina, the Common Ground Collective, co-founded by a former Black Panther under the motto 'solidarity, not charity', served everyone the flood had touched, and after Sandy, Occupy Sandy moved more volunteers through its hubs than the official agencies could field.

In 2020, hundreds of COVID mutual aid networks assembled within weeks and organised by building, block, and zip code rather than by identity, and in the 2025 Los Angeles fires, neighbourhood networks ran supply hubs for everyone displaced, including the undocumented residents whom federal relief excludes by rule.

Disaster sociology has replicated the pattern for six decades. Charles Fritz called the phenomenon a community of sufferers, defined by the event and not by the prior social system, and the Disaster Research Center's studies confirmed that the greater the disaster, the more such emergent groups appear.
argument.warrant: If the crossing had happened once, it would be an anecdote. It has recurred from 1793 to 2025, and disaster sociology has replicated it for six decades: catastrophe produces aid organised by the shared situation rather than by prior boundaries.
argument.qualifier: Everyday mutual aid in the nineteenth century mostly did run within communities, inside boundaries that were imposed at least as much as chosen. The claim is about what happens under pressure.
argument.rebuttal: One could object that disasters are exceptional moments, and that behaviour in an emergency proves nothing about the tradition in ordinary time.
argument.answer: But a practice that was inherently ethnic would stay ethnic under pressure, and it never has. Crisis strips the situation down to the tradition's actual organising principle, and that principle turns out to be need and presence.

nodes.label: C2 · Labour across lines
nodes.definition: Labour organising built mutual aid across ethnic lines, not only inside them.

grounds: Local 8 of the IWW, formed in the 1913 Philadelphia longshore strike, was roughly a third Black, a third Irish American, and a third immigrant Eastern European. It rotated its chairmanship between Black and white members, integrated work gangs on segregated docks, and controlled the waterfront for the better part of a decade.

The unions of that era were mutual aid institutions before they were bargaining agents. A local ran strike funds, sickness and death benefits, and relief for members' families, so organising across race meant pooling the machinery of survival, not only sharing a picket line.

The CIO drives of the 1930s and 1940s organised Black and white workers together in Southern tobacco plants, Memphis factories, and Midwestern packinghouses, in what historians of the period call civil rights unionism, a generation before the movement's famous years.

The cooperative movement ran the same experiment in economics. John Curl's history of American cooperation documents workers' cooperatives, buying clubs, and farmer alliances organising across ethnic lines, and where cooperative organising threatened the racial order it met violence: the cotton pickers' strike organised by the Colored Farmers' Alliance in 1891 was crushed.
argument.warrant: Aid follows the organising basis. Where the basis was the shared condition, the aid crossed race at dock, plant, and farm scale, and the crossings were not exceptions to the tradition but the tradition running on a wider definition of us.
argument.qualifier: Much of organised labour enforced the colour line rather than crossing it; the AFL's craft unions excluded Black workers for decades. The claim is about what happened where unions chose solidarity.
argument.rebuttal: One could object that interracial locals were rare islands in a labour movement that mostly practised exclusion.
argument.answer: But the exclusions prove the same rule. Where unions chose exclusion, aid stayed bounded and Black workers built parallel institutions. Where unions chose solidarity, the aid crossed immediately. The boundary tracked the choice, never the practice.

nodes.label: C3 · Institutions for everyone
nodes.definition: Some care institutions were deliberately built to serve beyond a single origin group.

grounds: In 1889, Hull House opened its doors to Chicago's Nineteenth Ward, the most ethnically mixed neighbourhood on the continent, running a kindergarten, a public kitchen, citizenship classes, and one of the city's first public playgrounds. The membership rule was the address rather than the origin.

The Black Panther breakfast tables fed every hungry child who walked in. The programmes were built by a Black organisation and rooted in Black neighbourhoods, but they were bounded by presence rather than by race, their own documents state that design plainly, and at their height they fed more children daily than some state governments.

The post-2020 networks made the same choice at city scale and said so in their founding documents. Bed-Stuy Strong's membership rule is the neighbourhood, the networks carrying groceries to Chinatown's seniors were staffed across racial lines, and Dean Spade's widely used definition of the practice contains no ethnic term.
argument.warrant: One place-bounded institution would be an outlier. The same design decision recurs in 1889, 1969, and 2020, which makes the non-ethnic form one of the tradition's recurring shapes rather than a modern innovation or an accident of emergency.
argument.qualifier: The settlement houses carry an honest caveat: funded by the wealthy, staffed by the educated, and never internally equal, they sit at the boundary between mutual aid and philanthropy. They demonstrate the design choice, not a pure case of the practice.
argument.rebuttal: One could object that these are hand-picked exceptions, and that most of the tradition's history still ran inside ethnic boundaries.
argument.answer: But the claim here is only that crossing the line was available and was chosen, repeatedly, in peacetime. Why so much of the history ran inside boundaries anyway is the next page's question, and the answer there is exclusion, not preference.

nodes.label: C4 · Exclusion, not principle
nodes.definition: Ethnic boundedness of many societies reflected the exclusion they were answering, not a principle that care is only for one's own.

grounds: In 1784, Prince Hall and fourteen other free Black Masons received their lodge charter from the Grand Lodge of England, because no American lodge would grant them one. The founding document of Black freemasonry crossed the Atlantic because it could not cross the street.

Nearly every ethnically bounded society has the same founding shape. The Free African Society organised among people excluded from Philadelphia's white congregations, the Grand United Order of Odd Fellows was chartered from England after the American order refused Black applicants, the landsmanshaftn multiplied among Jewish immigrants facing hostile institutions, and the Chinese family associations worked under the Chinese Exclusion Act.

The Historical Society of Pennsylvania states the mechanism in its own teaching materials: rising anti-immigrant and racist attitudes closed the established fraternals, and immigrants and African Americans 'were forced to form their own mutual aid associations'. The white orders wrote whites-only clauses into their constitutions.
argument.warrant: If the boundaries came from preference, they should persist wherever the practice persists. If they came from exclusion, the practice should cross lines whenever the exclusion lifts or the situation overrides it. The aid crossed every time the test ran.
argument.qualifier: Bounded societies were real, numerous, and often stayed bounded for generations. The claim explains why the boundary sat where it did, not that it did not exist.
argument.rebuttal: One could object that people simply prefer to care for their own kind, and that the ethnic societies are the natural shape of the practice.
argument.answer: But nearly every bounded society has the same founding story: a door closed first, and the society formed on the other side of it. The boundedness was the shape of the wall, traced from the inside.

nodes.label: D1 · Legal undermining
nodes.definition: Tax, food-sharing, and disaster rules actively undermine reciprocal aid while privileging registered charity.

grounds: Sharing food is repeatedly treated as an offence. A ninety-year-old veteran was charged three times in a month in 2014 for serving meals in a Fort Lauderdale park, a survey that year counted twenty-one cities restricting food sharing, and volunteers were still being arrested in Tulsa in 2026, despite a 2018 federal appeals ruling that sharing food in public is protected expressive conduct.

The tax code has no category for reciprocity. The researchers Shelly Sitton-Tygielski and Pamala Wiepking report that the tax-free gift is defined by a standard of 'detached and disinterested generosity' built for registered charity, that neighbours pooling money through payment apps can find the totals reported to the IRS as business income, and that most pandemic-era giving moved outside the registered-charity system entirely.

Eligibility rules draw the boundary from the other side. Federal disaster assistance requires citizenship or qualifying immigration status under the 1996 welfare reform, and in 2025 billions in disaster aid were held for immigration-enforcement review while a DHS directive moved to bar federally funded aid groups from serving undocumented residents.

The fourth mechanism is absorption. The fraternal benefit systems were displaced by commercial insurance and Social Security and vanished from the story of the safety net. And the geographer Nik Heynen writes that the Black Panther breakfast programme was 'both the model for, and impetus behind' the federally funded school breakfast programmes, which were made permanent in the same years in which documented COINTELPRO operations targeted the party.
argument.warrant: Any one of these mechanisms alone could be an accident of law. Four of them, taxation without recognition, attempted criminalisation, exclusion by eligibility, and absorption, all pressing in the same direction, describe a legal architecture with a consistent effect on reciprocal care.
argument.qualifier: Intent varies across the mechanisms: documented for COINTELPRO, debatable for the New Deal, and bureaucratically diffuse in the tax code. The claim is about the consistent structural effect, not a single conspiracy.
argument.rebuttal: One could object that these are scattered rules with separate rationales: public-order ordinances, tax administration, immigration law, and ordinary policy change.
argument.answer: But the rules keep arriving at the same result from every side. The courts keep siding with the volunteers and the cities keep passing ordinances anyway, while the dominant form of American generosity now operates in a legal architecture that does not recognise it.

nodes.label: D2 · Competing tradition
nodes.definition: A funded civic-nationalist tradition claimed the definition of American and pushed mutual aid out of the centre of the story.

grounds: In August 1971, Lewis Powell's confidential memorandum to the US Chamber of Commerce argued that business should build durable infrastructure in the places where public meaning is made: campuses, textbooks, television, and the courts. Much of the institutional world it called for was built within a decade, including the Heritage Foundation in 1973.

The construction is one of the best-documented episodes in modern American politics. Scholars have traced how the Olin, Scaife, Bradley, and Koch foundations funded think tanks, endowed law-school programmes, and built the Federalist Society's judicial pipeline, on the explicit theory that ideas need organisations and patrons to become common sense.

The reach figures come from the institutions themselves. Hillsdale College reports 1.7 million students enrolled in its free online curriculum and a circulation above 7.5 million for its speech digest, and the Heritage Foundation maintains a national library of free lesson plans on the founders and the Constitution.

On the other side of the shelf, the publicly available mutual aid teaching materials amount to a teaching guide attached to Dean Spade's 2020 book, an activist toolkit, and scattered lesson plans, none with published enrolment figures.
argument.warrant: Stories do not win on truth alone; they win on distribution. When one account of American identity has think tanks, curricula enrolling millions, and a judicial pipeline, and the other has scattered syllabi, the first becomes common sense by default.
argument.qualifier: That the infrastructure exists, was deliberately built, and mass-distributes a founding-documents account is documented fact. That it displaces the mutual aid tradition, rather than outcompeting it by default, is an interpretation, though a well-grounded one. Teaching the Constitution is legitimate.
argument.rebuttal: One could object that nobody suppressed the mutual aid story, and that the civic education infrastructure simply taught what its builders believed mattered.
argument.answer: But a tradition absent from every classroom, curriculum, and reference shelf is not one that citizens can find when they go looking for what being American means. Whatever the intent, teaching one account as the whole story produces exactly the invisibility that needed explaining.

nodes.label: D3 · Project 2025
nodes.definition: Project 2025 is the current culmination of that displacing tradition: eligibility, compliance, and a narrowed circle of care written as policy.

grounds: In 2023 the Heritage Foundation published Mandate for Leadership, the central document of Project 2025: roughly nine hundred pages of agency-by-agency policy design, prepared with more than a hundred advisory organisations and distributed free.

Its funders are substantially the same fortunes that built the civic education infrastructure. Grants from the Bradley, Scaife, Uihlein, Coors, Koch, and Seid fortunes to Project 2025's advisory organisations since 2020 total well over a hundred million dollars, documented in IRS filings.

Implementation is a matter of record from the plan's own author. In May 2026, Heritage president Kevin Roberts said on C-SPAN that 1,055 of 1,913 recommendations had been implemented, a Heritage fundraising email claimed 53 per cent was federal policy, and the independent Center for Progressive Reform tracker converges with that figure.

The policies bear directly on the tradition's ability to operate. A March 2025 executive order moved disaster preparedness away from FEMA, roughly ten billion dollars in disaster aid was held pending immigration-enforcement review, and an August 2025 DHS directive moved to bar federally funded aid groups from serving undocumented residents.
argument.warrant: When the plan's own author and its critics' tracker agree that more than half of it is federal policy, the document is no longer a wish list. It is the bounded-care account of the country, encoded in administration.
argument.qualifier: Project 2025 is a policy programme, and policy programmes are ordinary politics. The claim concerns what these particular policies do to the tradition's ability to operate, not that policy planning is illegitimate.
argument.rebuttal: One could object that administrations implement their supporters' agendas and think tanks write them, and that none of this is remarkable.
argument.answer: But these policies produce need, exclude the needy from state care, and burden the community care that remains, while the same legal order leaves the networks unrecognised by the tax code and, in some cities, criminalised. An architecture with that combined effect is not neutral about which American tradition survives.

nodes.label: D4 · Contestation
nodes.definition: The archive exists to contest that displacement by making the practice account citable civic knowledge.

grounds: The archive's strategy has a documented precedent in the rival tradition itself. A fifteen-thousand-dollar student conference in 1982 grew into the Federalist Society, with chapters at every accredited law school and, by 2024, six of the nine sitting Supreme Court justices among its members and affiliates, which is what a small, citable starting point can become.

The mechanism behind that precedent is studied. Constitutional originalism went from a single dismissed 1971 law review article to institutional dominance in roughly forty years, and Steven Teles's explanation is that ideas become power when they acquire networks, organisations, and patrons. The displacement this archive contests was built that way, so contesting it begins the same way: with a citable knowledge base.

Writing the record down is the tradition's own oldest act of self-defence. Jones and Allen published their Narrative in 1794 because the record was being falsified in real time, the AIDS generation named a political history Let the Record Show, and the historians of women's care networks recovered the practice diary by diary.
argument.warrant: If ideas become power only when they acquire networks, organisations, and patrons, then a tradition with no citable knowledge base cannot enter the contest at all. Assembling that base is the necessary first step, and the precedent shows the step can start that small.
argument.qualifier: A single document does not compete with a curriculum enrolling 1.7 million students, and this one does not claim to. The originalism precedent cuts both ways: the building takes decades.
argument.rebuttal: One could object that an archive is not a movement, and that documents change nothing by themselves.
argument.answer: But the tradition's own history answers this. The practice survived in memory partly because someone wrote it down each time. Care that goes unrecorded goes unremembered, and care that goes unremembered can be displaced without anyone noticing the loss.

nodes.label: Two accounts of belonging
nodes.definition: Belonging as practice (you are part of the community you show up for) versus belonging as condition (you belong if you qualify).

grounds: In April 1787, while the Constitutional Convention was meeting in Philadelphia, the Free African Society was founded in the same city. Its members paid dues to fund burials, sickness benefits, and support for widows. They built this system of mutual obligation because the official one excluded them.

This was not a one-off. Black benevolent and cooperative societies used the same dues-and-benefits design continuously from 1787 onward, and by the early twentieth century, fraternal orders built on that model enrolled roughly one in three adult American men.

The other tradition of belonging — belonging as a status you must qualify for — is just as real. It runs through American law from the Chinese Exclusion Act to today’s eligibility rules for public benefits.
argument.warrant: Both traditions are equally well documented and have run continuously since the founding. So when the national story remembers only one of them, that is a choice about what counts as American, not something the historical record forces on us.
argument.qualifier: This claim asks for equal standing, not a swap. The point is not that one tradition is false and the other true; both are real, and the argument is about which one gets remembered.
argument.rebuttal: One could object that mutual aid was a small thing: charity happening at the edges of society, not a serious rival to the official story of belonging.
argument.answer: But a tradition that enrolled one in three adult American men by 1920, and that provided the only insurance, credit, and burial systems millions of people had, was not a small thing. It did the work our national story gives credit to government and the market for doing.

nodes.label: COMMUNITY IS FABRIC
nodes.definition: Community is woven, not bounded. Weakness requires more weaving, not cutting threads.

nodes.label: BELONGING IS SHOWING UP
nodes.definition: You belong by what you do, not by what you are.

nodes.label: HELP IS SUPPORT
nodes.definition: Care is structural reinforcement. Helping strengthens the whole.
nodes.source: SUPPORT image schema (Lakoff & Johnson) — project reframe

nodes.label: CARE IS BUILDING
nodes.definition: Care work produces infrastructure rather than depleting a scarce resource.

nodes.label: SOLIDARITY IS STANDING TOGETHER
nodes.definition: Shared practice and proximity are commitment.

nodes.label: NATION IS CONTAINER
nodes.definition: The nation is a bounded vessel. Care is for those inside. Exclusion looks like geography.
nodes.source: Lakoff & Johnson 1980 (container schema); Lakoff, Moral Politics 1996

nodes.label: MORALITY IS ACCOUNTING
nodes.definition: Moral worth is a balance sheet. Care is a withdrawal you must have paid in for.

nodes.label: CARE IS EXCHANGE
nodes.definition: Care is a commodity. Receiving without paying is freeloading.

nodes.label: CARE IS CHARITY
nodes.definition: Care flows one way, from benefactor to beneficiary. Reciprocal obligation is invisible.
nodes.source: Conventional cultural model, named in the Phase 1 linguistic reframe

nodes.label: CARE IS A SCARCE RESOURCE
nodes.definition: Care is finite and zero-sum. Exclusion reads as rationing.
nodes.source: Zero-sum resource metaphor — Phase 1 linguistic reframe

nodes.label: Collaboration
nodes.definition: Partners work together. No benefactor. Roles are reciprocal.

nodes.label: Building
nodes.definition: An agent creates a structure from components. Care as construction.

nodes.label: Eligibility
nodes.definition: Access depends on meeting criteria. Naming it activates gating.
nodes.source: FrameNet-style gating frame — Phase 1 frame inventory

nodes.label: Compliance
nodes.definition: A party must satisfy a rule to remain in good standing.

nodes.label: Crisis response
nodes.definition: Neighbours organise when the official system lags. Opens the reframe without a partisan argument.
nodes.source: Project catalytic frame — Phase 1 listening model

nodes.label: Tradition
nodes.definition: A practice is old and repeated. 'We always have.'
nodes.source: FrameNet: Custom — catalytic use per Phase 1 listening model

nodes.label: A · Founding tradition
nodes.definition: Mutual aid is a founding American tradition: present at the founding, built as civic infrastructure, and operating at national scale by 1920.

nodes.label: B · Survival through American identity
nodes.definition: The tradition survived the twentieth century by carrying excluded communities through crises the state and market would not meet.

nodes.label: C · Not only in-group
nodes.definition: The practice repeatedly crossed group lines; where it was bounded, the boundary reflected exclusion, not a principle of care for one’s own only.

nodes.label: D · Displacement and contest
nodes.definition: A funded rival account displaced mutual aid from the American story, and that displacement is contestable in the present.
